title: At the café
goal: Order food and drinks at three levels of politeness, and ask what's in a dish — including the question many readers of this course need most.
bekal: name thirty foods and drinks you'll really find in an Estonian café
ask what a dish contains and politely decline

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Kohvik vanalinnas
dialogs.intro: Kerli takes Budi to a café in Tallinn's Old Town.

lines.speaker: Kerli:
lines.text: Jah. Mulle üks suur latte ja üks saiake, palun.
lines.id: Yes. A large latte for me and a sweet bun.
lines.literal: yes. me-to one large latte and one bun, please.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Ma sooviksin teed. Kas teil on rohelist teed?
lines.id: I'd like tea. Do you have green tea?
lines.literal: I want-would-I tea-PARTITIVE. [question] you(pl)-at is green-PARTITIVE tea-PARTITIVE?

lines.speaker: Ettekandja:
lines.text: Jah, on küll. Kas soovite ka midagi süüa?
lines.id: Yes, we do. Would you like something to eat too?
lines.literal: yes, is indeed. [question] want-you(pl) also something to-eat?

lines.speaker: Kerli:
lines.text: Ei ole. See on magus, kohupiimast ja šokolaadist.
lines.id: No. It's sweet, made of curd cheese and chocolate.
lines.literal: not is. that is-it sweet, curd-milk-from and chocolate-from.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Siis ma võtan ühe. Ja ka klaasi vett, palun.
lines.id: Then I'll take one. And a glass of water too, please.
lines.literal: then I take-I one-GEN. and also glass-GEN water-PARTITIVE, please.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Palun. Kas siin on vaba laud?
lines.id: Here you are. Is there a free table?

lines.speaker: Ettekandja:
lines.text: Jah, akna kõrval. Palun võtke istet!
lines.id: Yes, by the window. Please take a seat!
lines.literal: yes, window-GEN beside. please take seat-PARTITIVE!

notes: **Mulle, teile** — "for me", "for you". When ordering, Estonians often just say *mulle* + the item with no verb at all: *Mulle üks kohv, palun.* ("One coffee for me, please.") This is the shortest order and perfectly polite.

**Rohelis*t* tee*d*.** Notice that **the adjective changes too**, to match its noun: *roheline tee* becomes *rohelist teed*. This holds throughout Estonian — adjectives always copy the form of their noun (English adjectives never change, so this is new). Covered in Unit 14.

**Midagi süüa** — "something to eat". *Süüa* is the second form of the verb "to eat"; the first is *sööma*. Estonian has **two basic forms** for every verb, and which one is used depends on the words before it. Covered in Unit 10 — don't chase it now.

**Klaasi vett** — "a glass of water". The container is in the genitive (*klaas* → *klaasi*), the contents in the partitive (*vesi* → *vett*). Same pattern: *tass kohvi* (a cup of coffee), *pudel veini* (a bottle of wine), *taldrik suppi* (a plate of soup).

grammars.title: Three ways to order, from the shortest
body: All of them are polite. The difference isn't politeness but how careful you sound.

head: Form
Example
Feels
When to use it
rows: Confident, you know what you want
Asking for something off the menu.

after: The last two forms use the **conditional** (*-ksin*), the equivalent of English "would" or "could". You don't need to understand the form yet — just memorize *ma sooviksin* ("I would like") and *kas ma saaksin* ("could I have") as whole phrases. The form is unpacked in Unit 19.
⚠️ Don't add *palun* to every sentence. Estonian doesn't use it as often as English uses "please", and repeating *palun* three times in one order sounds odd. Once at the end is enough.

grammars.title: ⚠️ Why the drinks change form
body: Notice this pattern all through the dialogue: *tee* becomes *teed*, *vesi* becomes *vett*, *kohv* becomes *kohvi*. The second form is called the **partitive**, and the reason makes sense once you say it aloud: you're not ordering **all the tea in the world**, you're ordering some of it — like English "some tea".
after: A practical rule for now: **things you can't count one by one — liquids, materials, shapeless food — almost always take the partitive.** That already covers nearly the whole café menu.

Compare countable things: *Ma võtan ühe saiakese* (I'll take one bun) — this uses the **genitive**, because the whole bun is taken. The difference is covered fully in Unit 13; don't force yourself to grasp it now.
If in doubt, **use the partitive**. In a café, a mistake in that direction almost never sounds wrong.

blocks.title: Three Estonian foods you'll be offered
items: *kohuke* — a chocolate-covered curd-cheese bar, sold in every shop. Sweet, cold, and completely meat-free. The real national snack.
*must leib* — dense, slightly sour dark rye bread. Estonians living abroad miss this more than anything.
*kama* — a flour blend of four grains, stirred with sour milk. It tastes strange at the first bite; give it a second chance.
⚠️ *verivorst* (blood sausage) turns up everywhere at Christmas. If you have dietary restrictions, learn its name.

blocks.text: Estonia is not a country used to religious dietary rules, and pork is in many everyday dishes — often without being named. The sentences below are not extras; for many readers of this course they are the most useful part of the unit.

blocks.title: Words to recognize on labels
items: *sealiha* — pork. Literally "pig meat" (*siga* = pig). ⚠️ This is the most important word on this page.
*peekon* — bacon. *sink* — ham. *vorst* — sausage. All three are almost always pork unless stated otherwise.
*alkohol* — alcohol. *alkoholivaba* — alcohol-free. ⚠️ The ending *-vaba* means "free of": *gluteenivaba*, *laktoosivaba*, *suhkruvaba*.

blocks.text: The ending **-vaba** is worth memorizing right now. It attaches to any word and means "without" (like English "-free"), so you can read labels you've never seen: *lihavaba* (meat-free), *piimavaba* (dairy-free). Compare the prefix *eba-* in Unit 3 — Estonian likes to build words from parts you can re-attach.

⚠️ About tipping: in Estonia tips are **not required** and not expected. In a restaurant, rounding up or leaving five to ten percent is considered generous; in an ordinary café, leaving nothing is completely normal. Don't feel obliged.
